items.q: You committed an API key, then in the next commit you deleted the line. Is the key safe now?
options: No — git history keeps the old commit, so the key is still recoverable and must be rotated
Only unsafe if you pushed within the last 24 hours
Yes — it's gone from the current code
Yes, as long as the repo is private

explain.right: Git history retains the committed value; deleting the line later doesn't remove it. Treat the key as leaked and rotate it.
explain.wrong: Deleting the line, a private repo, or the timing don't help — the value lives in history and must be revoked/rotated.

items.q: Why is putting a key in your source code dangerous, even in a private repo?
options: It slows the program down
It only matters for payment keys
It makes the file larger
Anyone with repo access (now or later) can read and use it, and private repos leak, fork, or get published by mistake

explain.right: A key in the repo is readable by everyone with access and survives in history; private repos still leak, and automated scanners harvest public ones in minutes.
explain.wrong: It's not about file size or speed, and all keys matter — any credential grants access or costs money.

items.q: What's the right place for a secret the code needs?
options: In the environment — a gitignored .env locally, or a secret manager/env vars in production — with the code referencing it by name
In the repo's README so collaborators can see it
In a comment at the top of the file so it's easy to find
Hard-coded in the file, but base64-encoded so it looks scrambled

explain.right: Keep the value out of the code and in the environment; the code asks for it by name. Commit a value-free .env.example to document the names.
explain.wrong: Base64 is encoding, not encryption — it's trivially reversible and not secret; comments and READMEs are still in the repo.

items.q: Which pair of habits best limits the damage when a key eventually leaks?
options: Use the same powerful key everywhere so there's less to manage
Make the key longer, and never tell anyone it exists
Store two copies in case one is lost
Scope the key to least privilege (only what it needs) and rotate it (replace + revoke) on any suspected leak

explain.right: Least privilege shrinks the blast radius, and rotation makes a stolen key stop working — together they make a leak survivable.
explain.wrong: Length and secrecy don't help once it's stolen, extra copies add exposure, and one all-powerful key maximizes the damage.

items.q: A teammate says 'I base64-encoded the password in the config, so it's protected.' What's the correct response?
options: Base64 is encoding, not encryption; anyone can reverse it instantly, so the secret is still exposed — move it out of the config
Great — base64 is a solid encryption step
Add a second base64 pass to make it stronger
It's fine as long as the config isn't committed

explain.right: Encoding (base64) just changes representation and is trivially reversible; it provides zero secrecy. The secret belongs in the environment, not the config.
explain.wrong: Base64 isn't encryption and double-encoding adds nothing; even uncommitted, a plaintext-equivalent secret in config is the wrong place.
